---
title: "2.9 — General completeness of first-order resolution"
---

```lean
import Principia.FirstOrder
open Principia.FirstOrder
```

## 1. The question: could an unsatisfiable clause set have no refutation?

Soundness rules out refutations of satisfiable inputs. Completeness supplies the other
direction: every unsatisfiable clause set has a finite refutation. We prove this for arbitrary
first-order clauses, including function symbols that generate infinitely many terms.

Our proof proceeds contrapositively. If no refutation exists, build a model. This shares the
shape of Henkin completeness, but clauses need no existential witness construction: their
variables are already implicitly universal.

## 2. Make the structural rules explicit

The certificate type includes two structural rules in addition to input, substitution,
resolution, and contraction:

- `weakening` adds disjuncts. From A, deriving A ∨ B is sound; it does not establish B.
- `tautology l` supplies the universally true clause [l, l.complement].

```lean
def addAlternative (s : ClauseSet) (l k : Literal)
    (d : ResolutionDerivation s [l]) : ResolutionDerivation s [l, k] := by
  exact .weakening d (by simp_all)
```

These are ordinary structural rules, with checked soundness proofs. They simplify the
assumption-discharge argument in our completeness proof. The theorem below concerns this
explicit six-constructor calculus; it does not silently assert completeness for a smaller
or differently implemented system.

## 3. Treat every substitution instance as a propositional clause

`InstanceSource S c` says that c is some substitution instance of an input clause of S.
There may be infinitely many such clauses, even when S is finite. For P(x) with a constant
c and unary f, examples include P(c), P(f(c)), P(f(f(c))), and so on.

Each such instance has an actual first-order derivation: take its input leaf and add the
recorded substitution node. `resolution_of_propositional` translates a finite resolution
tree using these instances back into a first-order resolution certificate.

The proof does not require the unifier to return a most-general substitution: instantiation
is an explicit rule. This avoids assuming an unproved MGU or lifting theorem for our bounded
unification program. It also means calculus completeness alone is not search completeness.

## 4. Build a consistent Boolean assignment for all instance atoms

A finite resolution tree uses only finitely many source clauses. We build a sequence of
consistent extensions deciding more and more atoms. The enumeration covers every finite
term and every atom; it puts no fixed ceiling on function nesting.

The key step discharges a temporary unit assumption. If T together with [l] refutes the
empty clause, `Propositional.Proof.deduction` gives a proof from T of [l.complement].
If adding either sign caused a refutation, the two discharged unit proofs would resolve
to the empty clause already from T. Hence one sign can safely be chosen.

This consistency choice is noncomputable. It constructs a mathematical assignment; it is
not an algorithm deciding satisfiability of an infinite set of instances.

For an original instance clause, suppose every literal were false in the resulting assignment.
There are only finitely many literals, so all their complementary unit decisions occur together
at some finite stage. Resolve against those units one by one: the clause becomes empty.
That contradicts the stage's consistency. Every instance clause must therefore be satisfied.

## 5. Read the assignment as a first-order term model

Use all finite terms as domain. Interpret functions by forming term trees, and interpret
a predicate on term objects using the assignment to that exact atom.

An environment maps each variable to a term object. Evaluating an input clause in this model
is exactly evaluating its substitution instance propositionally. We just proved that every
such instance is satisfied, so every input clause holds under every environment.

The theorem `model_of_no_refutation` supplies this canonical model. Contrapositively:

```text
resolution_complete : Unsatisfiable S → Nonempty (ResolutionDerivation S [])
resolution_iff_unsatisfiable S :
  Nonempty (ResolutionDerivation S []) ↔ Unsatisfiable S
```

These are general, kernel-checked first-order results. They concern existence of finite trees,
not eventual success of the current bounded saturation strategy. That program still returns
unknown when it finds no refutation. Lesson 2.8 proves the clausifier's general equisatisfiability,
so a refutation of the generated counterexample clauses certifies the original entailment.

### The complete bridge to natural deduction

For arbitrary Γ and goal, the library now proves:

```text
deduction_iff_clausal_refutation Γ goal :
  Nonempty (Derivation Γ goal) ↔
    Nonempty (ResolutionDerivation
      (clausify (counterexampleFormula Γ goal)).clauses [])
```

A natural-deduction proof establishes entailment by soundness. That entailment excludes any
model of the counterexample formula. Recovery of a model from its generated clauses therefore
shows those clauses are unsatisfiable; resolution completeness supplies a refutation.

Conversely, a clause refutation excludes all models of those clauses. Any original countermodel
would expand to one, contradicting the refutation. Hence entailment holds, and natural-deduction
completeness supplies a derivation. Every link is checked; no clausification hypothesis is left
for the caller to assume. This is an existence equivalence between proof systems, not a theorem
that our particular finite searches always find their certificates.

## 6. Prove it

Work in `Skeleton.lean`. These exercises apply the new ideas to statements different from
the worked examples. Try them before reading the corrections.

```bash
make lab C=02-resolution/09-first-order-completeness
```

An unsatisfiable subsystem is included in a larger clause set. Show the larger set has a refutation.

```lean
theorem refutation_of_unsatisfiable_subsystem (s t : ClauseSet)
    (included : ∀ c ∈ s, c ∈ t) (h : Unsatisfiable s) :
    Nonempty (ResolutionDerivation t []) := by
  sorry
```

Turn absence of a finite refutation into existence of a first-order model on terms.

```lean
theorem consistent_source_has_term_model (s : ClauseSet)
    (h : ¬Nonempty (ResolutionDerivation s [])) :
    ∃ M : Model Term, SatisfiesClauses M s := by
  sorry
```

## 7. Graduated hints

### `refutation_of_unsatisfiable_subsystem`

**First hint.** Any model of t would also model s.

**Next hint.** Establish Unsatisfiable t, then apply resolution_complete.

### `consistent_source_has_term_model`

**First hint.** Use the canonical model from the contrapositive proof.

**Next hint.** The witness is canonicalModel s and its property is model_of_no_refutation h.

## 8. Worked corrections

These exact proofs are also in `Solution.lean`, checked by `make test`.

### `refutation_of_unsatisfiable_subsystem`

```lean
theorem refutation_of_unsatisfiable_subsystem (s t : ClauseSet)
    (included : ∀ c ∈ s, c ∈ t) (h : Unsatisfiable s) :
    Nonempty (ResolutionDerivation t []) := by
  apply resolution_complete
  intro D inhabited M ht
  exact h D inhabited M (fun c hc => ht c (included c hc))
```

A model satisfying every clause of t satisfies each clause of s by inclusion. The hypothesis rules out that model. General completeness then supplies a finite refutation of t.

### `consistent_source_has_term_model`

```lean
theorem consistent_source_has_term_model (s : ClauseSet)
    (h : ¬Nonempty (ResolutionDerivation s [])) :
    ∃ M : Model Term, SatisfiesClauses M s :=
  ⟨canonicalModel s, model_of_no_refutation h⟩
```

canonicalModel interprets functions as term constructors and predicates through the consistent assignment. The model-existence theorem proves that it satisfies every original clause at every environment.

## 9. Optional practice

Use `optional/Skeleton.lean`. Pending optional proofs are reported separately and do not
fail completed required work.

Show an arbitrary source containing complementary units is inconsistent.

```lean
theorem incompatible_units_inconsistent (T : Clause → Prop) (l : Literal)
    (positive : T [l]) (negative : T [l.complement]) : ¬Propositional.Consistent T := by
  sorry
```

*Hint:* Resolve the two available unit clauses and contradict consistency.

Show clause sets with exactly the same models have exactly the same refutability status.

```lean
theorem semantic_refutability_invariant (s t : ClauseSet)
    (sameModels : ∀ (D : Type) (_ : Nonempty D) (M : Model D),
      SatisfiesClauses M s ↔ SatisfiesClauses M t) :
    Nonempty (ResolutionDerivation s []) ↔ Nonempty (ResolutionDerivation t []) := by
  sorry
```

*Hint:* Use the general equivalence on both sides, then transport models in the appropriate direction.

## 10. Optional corrections

These proofs are in `optional/Solution.lean`, included in the checks and exercise reset.

### `incompatible_units_inconsistent`

```lean
theorem incompatible_units_inconsistent (T : Clause → Prop) (l : Literal)
    (positive : T [l]) (negative : T [l.complement]) : ¬Propositional.Consistent T := by
  intro consistent
  apply consistent
  exact ⟨by simpa [resolvent] using
    Propositional.Proof.resolve l (.input positive) (.input negative)⟩
```

The two input leaves have opposite signs. Resolving their singleton clauses produces the empty clause, which the consistency predicate excludes.

### `semantic_refutability_invariant`

```lean
theorem semantic_refutability_invariant (s t : ClauseSet)
    (sameModels : ∀ (D : Type) (_ : Nonempty D) (M : Model D),
      SatisfiesClauses M s ↔ SatisfiesClauses M t) :
    Nonempty (ResolutionDerivation s []) ↔ Nonempty (ResolutionDerivation t []) := by
  rw [resolution_iff_unsatisfiable, resolution_iff_unsatisfiable]
  constructor
  · intro hs D inhabited M ht
    exact hs D inhabited M ((sameModels D inhabited M).mpr ht)
  · intro ht D inhabited M hs
    exact ht D inhabited M ((sameModels D inhabited M).mp hs)
```

General completeness and soundness replace syntactic refutability by unsatisfiability. In each direction, use the sameModels equivalence to translate a purported model into the model forbidden by the hypothesis.

## 11. Conclusion

The explicit resolution calculus is sound and refutation-complete for arbitrary finite first-order clause sets. All substitution instances and the canonical term model establish the general result without assuming MGU completeness of the bounded unifier. Completeness of a calculus, completeness of its search strategy, and correctness of a formula-to-clause compiler are separate claims.
